372.title: My own size
372.hook: take a role beyond your powers and you fail it and neglect the one you could have filled (Enchiridion 37)
372.howItsDone: People practicing Stoicism sometimes review their commitments and decline roles beyond their present powers, to protect the roles they already hold.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the biggest portion, and the fellowship of the shared meal. Your line was the table matters. Who did you let choose first? Day three hundred seventy-two.

The email says: we were hoping you'd chair the committee. You're flattered. You're also already behind on everything, you've never run a budget, and the committee meets on the night you usually put your kids to bed. You say yes anyway. Six months later the committee is struggling, and so is bedtime. Section thirty-seven of the handbook is a single sentence. It describes that six months exactly, and it names both things that went wrong. Today: my own size.
screen: `WE HOPED YOU'D CHAIR THE COMMITTEE.` → `YOU SAY YES ANYWAY.` → `MY OWN SIZE.`

segments.voice: First, the line. If you take on a role beyond your powers, Epictetus says, you disgrace yourself in it, and you neglect the role you could have filled. Two losses, not one. Second, the word for role. The Greek is prosōpon. It meant a face, and then an actor's mask, and then the part the mask stood for. We met this picture back in section seventeen: you're an actor in a play someone else wrote, and your job is to play your part well. Today adds the other side. Don't grab a part that isn't yours. Latin used persona for the same idea, mask and role together, and Cicero, drawing on an earlier Stoic, built a whole theory of the roles each of us plays. Third, the double cost. The first loss is obvious: the role you weren't ready for goes badly, and people see it. The second loss is quieter and usually bigger. The part that really was yours, the friend, the parent, the craftsman, the neighbor, gets the leftovers. Nobody throws a party for a role you neglected. It just thins out. Fourth, what this isn't. It isn't a rule to stay small forever. In a couple of weeks the handbook will ask, sharply, how long you're going to wait to become your best. Growth is welcome. The point is honesty about your present size: what you can carry now, what you're for right now, and which yes would cost a part you've already been given.
screen: `A ROLE BEYOND YOUR POWERS.` · `PROSŌPON: FACE, MASK, ROLE.` · `TWO LOSSES: THAT ROLE, AND YOURS.` · `HONEST ABOUT YOUR PRESENT SIZE.` · then, large: `MY OWN SIZE.`

segments.voice: Settle, and breathe. Think of what you've said yes to lately, the invitations, the asks, the jobs you took because nobody else would. Is there one that's beyond your powers right now, or that keeps eating time from a part that really is yours? Don't solve it. Just name it. Then picture saying, kindly and clearly: I'm not the right person for this. Notice what loosens. The bell holds the time.
My own size. Epictetus: take a role beyond your powers and you fail it, and neglect the one you could have filled. Today's word.
Your line: my own size. Decline one role today that isn't yours, kindly, so the parts that are yours get your best. Day three hundred seventy-two.

373.title: Mind the step
373.hook: as you watch for nails when walking, watch over your ruling mind (Enchiridion 38)
373.howItsDone: Some people practicing Stoicism use slow, attentive walking as a reminder to pause before accepting a judgment, guarding the mind as carefully as their footing.

segments.voice: Yesterday: a role beyond your powers, and the part it pushes aside. Your line was my own size. Which role did you decline, or wish you had? Day three hundred seventy-three.

Walk barefoot across a garage floor and watch what happens to you. Nobody has to tell you to pay attention. Your eyes go to every step. Your weight hangs back for a beat before each foot lands, just in case there's a nail, a screw, a sharp bit of glass. You do it without thinking, because you know what a nail in the foot feels like. Section thirty-eight of the handbook takes that ordinary carefulness and points it somewhere new. Today: mind the step.
screen: `BAREFOOT ON A GARAGE FLOOR.` → `EVERY STEP WATCHED.` → `MIND THE STEP.`

segments.voice: First, the line. Just as when you walk you take care not to step on a nail or twist your foot, Epictetus says, take care in the same way not to harm your ruling mind. And if we watched for this in every action, we'd go about each one more safely. Second, today's word. The Greek is hēgemonikon, the ruling part. It's related to hēgemōn, a leader or guide. For the Stoics, the hēgemonikon was the command center of a person, the place where impressions are received, judged, and given or refused assent. Chrysippus, one of the school's early heads, even placed it in the heart. Marcus Aurelius uses the word again and again in his private notebook. Third, the nail. Notice how much care we already give the body without effort. We watch for nails, wipe up spills, check the stairs in the dark. Epictetus is asking for the same easy care for the part of us that decides. Fourth, what a nail looks like for the mind. A judgment made in a rush. A resentment you agree to without checking. An impression, he's rude, I'm a failure, it's ruined, accepted at face value. Each one is a small injury to the ruling part, and like a foot injury, it changes how you walk for a while afterward. The fix isn't fear. It's attention at the moment of stepping: a beat before agreeing to the thought, the way you hang back before your foot lands.
screen: `WATCH THE MIND AS YOU WATCH YOUR FEET.` · `HĒGEMONIKON: THE RULING PART.` · `WE ALREADY GUARD THE BODY.` · `A RUSHED JUDGMENT IS A NAIL.` · then, large: `MIND THE STEP.`

segments.voice: If you can stand, stand up and walk, slowly, for the length of the bell. Feel the heel, the ball of the foot, the toes. Let each step be watched, the way you'd cross a floor with nails on it. If you're sitting, rest your feet flat and feel them press the floor. Either way, notice a thought arriving, and give it the same beat you give a step: look before you agree. The bell holds the time.
Hēgemonikon. The Stoic word for the ruling part of the mind, where impressions are judged. Guard it, Epictetus says, as you guard your feet. Today's word.
Your line: mind the step. Walk carefully for three minutes today, every step watched, and give one hasty thought the same beat. Day three hundred seventy-three.

374.title: The foot measures the shoe
374.hook: the body is the measure of what you need, as the foot is of the shoe (Enchiridion 39)
374.howItsDone: Some people practicing Stoicism use the body's actual needs as a measure for buying and owning, and notice when a want has gone past what the body asks for.

segments.voice: Yesterday: hēgemonikon, the ruling mind, guarded like a foot on a garage floor. Your line was mind the step. Which hasty thought did you catch before it landed? Day three hundred seventy-four.

Open a closet and count the shoes. Not to judge. Just count. Then count your feet. Two, for most of us. Somewhere between those two numbers there's a story. A pair for running. Then a nicer pair for running. Then a pair that matches the jacket. Epictetus, who by tradition lived with very little, looked at the humble shoe and saw a whole philosophy of having. Section thirty-nine is short. Today: the foot measures the shoe.
screen: `COUNT THE SHOES.` → `NOW COUNT YOUR FEET.` → `THE FOOT MEASURES THE SHOE.`

segments.voice: First, the measure. The body, Epictetus says, is the measure of what each person needs to own, as the foot is the measure of the shoe. A shoe has a job, and the foot tells you when it's done. Food, clothing, shelter: the body tells you, roughly, how much is enough. Second, the edge. If you stop there, he says, you'll keep the measure. But if you step past it, you'll be carried along as if over a cliff. Past the measure, there's no natural place to stop. Third, the slide, told with a shoe. Once you go beyond what the foot needs, he says, the shoe becomes gilded, then purple, then embroidered. Hear the ladder in those three words: plain leather becomes a show. Each step makes sense once you've taken the one before it. And nothing on the ladder ever says: that's enough. Fourth, why the body is such a good measure. It comes with you. It doesn't read advertisements. It gets full, it gets warm, it gets dry, and then it's done. Desire has no such signal. Epicurus, who led a rival school, made a similar point in his own way: what nature needs is limited and easy to get, while what empty opinion wants has no limit. Two schools, each with its own reasons, pointing at the same quiet fact. Enough is a real thing. The foot already knows where it is.
screen: `THE BODY IS THE MEASURE OF HAVING.` · `PAST IT, OVER A CLIFF.` · `GILDED, THEN PURPLE, THEN EMBROIDERED.` · `THE BODY KNOWS ENOUGH; DESIRE DOESN'T.` · then, large: `THE FOOT MEASURES.`

segments.voice: Settle, and breathe. Feel your feet where they rest. Feel the clothes on your body, the seat under you, the air in the room. For this minute, the body has what it needs. Now think of one thing you own more than enough of, or one thing you've been wanting that the body isn't asking for. Just notice it. Then come back to your feet, and to the plain feeling of enough. The bell holds the time.
The foot measures the shoe. Epictetus: the body is the measure of what you need to own. Past it, there's no place to stop. Today's word.
screen: `THE FOOT MEASURES THE SHOE — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: the foot measures. Notice one enough today: a meal, a closet, a cart, a screen, where the body says done. Day three hundred seventy-four.

375.title: Honor the character
375.hook: girls flattered for looks from fourteen should learn they're honored for self-respect (Enchiridion 40)
375.howItsDone: Some people practicing Stoicism make a habit of praising others, especially children, for character and effort rather than appearance, following Epictetus' point in Enchiridion 40.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the shoe that slides from gilded to purple to embroidered. Your line was the foot measures. Where did you notice enough? Day three hundred seventy-five.

Listen to what grown-ups say to children at a family party. To the little boys: you're so strong, you're so fast. To the little girls, again and again: look how pretty you are. It's meant kindly. But children pick up what the adults around them value, often from exactly these small remarks. Epictetus noticed the same thing in his own world, and wrote it down in a section of the handbook that's short, and a little uncomfortable, and still sharp. Today: honor the character.
screen: `STRONG, FAST. PRETTY.` → `CHILDREN LEARN WHAT WE VALUE.` → `HONOR THE CHARACTER.`

segments.voice: First, his world. In section forty Epictetus says that from about fourteen, girls are flattered by men and called ladies. Seeing that they're valued for nothing except their appeal to men, he says, they begin to dress up and put all their hopes in that. Second, his answer. It's worth taking care, he says, that they come to understand they're honored for nothing else than being decent and self-respecting. Not for looks. For character. That's the whole section. Third, an honest note. This chapter is written about girls, by a man, in a society that gave women little say over their own lives, and some modern readers find parts of its framing dated. But the core sentence points a finger at the people doing the flattering as much as at the girls, and it says plainly that a young woman's worth is in her character. Stoic teachers before him, like Musonius Rufus, Epictetus' own teacher, argued that women should study philosophy too. Fourth, why it reaches us. The praise we give teaches people what they're worth. Praise only looks, and you teach someone to put their hopes in a mirror, which time will eventually disappoint. Praise honesty, kindness, courage, effort, and you point them at the part of themselves nobody can take away. In Stoic terms, you praise what's up to them. That works for boys, for adults, for anyone. It just takes a little more attention than noticing a haircut.
screen: `FLATTERED FOR LOOKS FROM FOURTEEN.` · `HONORED FOR SELF-RESPECT.` · `DATED FRAME, SHARP CORE.` · `PRAISE WHAT'S UP TO THEM.` · then, large: `HONOR THE CHARACTER.`

segments.voice: Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind someone you'll see soon: a child, a friend, a coworker, a partner. Set aside how they look. Ask instead: what have I seen in their character lately? Patience with a hard customer. Honesty when it cost something. Kindness nobody else noticed. Find one, and find the words you'd use to name it, plainly. Hold those words ready. The bell holds the time.
Honor the character. Enchiridion forty: people should learn they're honored for decency and self-respect, not looks. Today's word.
Your line: honor the character. Praise one person today for character, not looks: name something they did that was up to them. Day three hundred seventy-five.

376.title: Mind first
376.hook: spending too long on the body is a sign of neglecting the mind (Enchiridion 41)
376.howItsDone: Some people practicing Stoicism keep the body's routines simple and set aside a few deliberate minutes each day for reading, reflection or journaling.

segments.voice: Yesterday: praise that teaches people what they're worth. Your line was honor the character. Whose character did you name out loud? Day three hundred seventy-six.

Add it up for one ordinary day. The workout. The shower and the hair. The meals, the snacks, the planning of meals. The skincare, the mirror, the step count on the watch. Now add up the minutes that went to the mind on purpose: thinking something through, reading something that stretched you, asking whether a judgment was true. Which list is longer? Epictetus doesn't ask you to drop the first one. He asks you to look at the ratio. Today: mind first.
screen: `ADD UP THE BODY'S MINUTES.` → `NOW THE MIND'S.` → `MIND FIRST.`

segments.voice: First, the line. It's a sign of a dull nature, Epictetus says, to spend a lot of time on the things of the body: a lot of exercise, a lot of eating, a lot of drinking, and the rest of the body's business. Second, the key word is a lot. He isn't against the body. His own teacher, Musonius Rufus, taught that students should train the body as well as the soul, through cold and heat and hard work. Epictetus doesn't forbid eating, drinking or exercise either. He asks you to notice when the body's business takes up the whole day. These things, he says, should be done in passing, along the way. Third, where the attention goes instead. All your care, he says, should turn toward the mind. The Greek here is gnōmē, a word for judgment, outlook, the way a person thinks things through. For the Stoics, that's where a life actually gets lived: in how you judge what happens. A well-tended body with a neglected mind is like a beautifully kept house where no one ever opens the windows. Fourth, why it's urgent and not just nice. The body will be looked after whether you plan it or not. Hunger reminds you. Tiredness reminds you. Nothing in the day reminds you to think. The mind only gets its turn if you give it one on purpose. That's why the handbook tilts so hard in one direction. Not because the body doesn't matter, but because the mind is the one that gets forgotten.
screen: `TOO MUCH TIME ON THE BODY.` · `DO THE BODY'S THINGS IN PASSING.` · `GNŌMĒ: TURN YOUR CARE TO THE MIND.` · `NOTHING REMINDS YOU TO THINK.` · then, large: `MIND FIRST.`

segments.voice: Settle, and breathe. Let the body be looked after for a minute: let it sit, let it breathe. Now give the mind its turn. Pick one question that deserves real thought. Something you believe and have never checked. A decision you keep putting off. A line from this handbook that bothered you. Turn it over slowly, the way you'd turn a stone in your hand. No need to answer it. Just think on purpose. The bell holds the time.
Mind first. Enchiridion forty-one: do the body's business in passing, and turn your real care toward the mind. Today's word.
Your line: mind first. Give five minutes to the mind today on purpose: a page that stretches you, or one question thought all the way through. Day three hundred seventy-six.

377.title: It seemed right to him
377.hook: when someone wrongs you, remember he did what seemed right to him (Enchiridion 42)
377.howItsDone: People practicing Stoicism often remind themselves, when wronged, that the other person acted on what seemed right to them, which helps them respond without adding anger.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the body's business in passing, and real care for the mind. Your line was mind first. What did you give your five minutes to? Day three hundred seventy-seven.

Someone cuts you off in traffic, and in the half second before the horn, a whole story forms in your head about who they are. Selfish. Reckless. Probably like this all the time. Hardly anyone pauses to tell the other story: that from inside that car, the move made sense. Late for a shift. A kid crying in the back. A misjudged mirror. Or simply a belief that the lane was theirs. Section forty-two of the handbook asks you to tell that second story, every time. Today: it seemed right to him.
screen: `CUT OFF IN TRAFFIC.` → `A WHOLE STORY IN HALF A SECOND.` → `IT SEEMED RIGHT TO HIM.`

segments.voice: First, the line. When someone treats you badly or speaks badly of you, Epictetus says, remember that he does it or says it because he thinks it's right for him to. He can't act on what seems right to you. Only on what seems right to him. Second, who gets hurt. If what seemed right to him is wrong, he says, then he's the one harmed, because he's the one who was deceived. Epictetus gives an example from logic. If someone takes a true statement to be false, the statement isn't harmed. The person who got it wrong is. Third, the old root. This goes back to an idea often traced to Socrates, in Plato's dialogues: that nobody does wrong knowingly, believing it to be wrong. People act on what looks good to them, even when it isn't. The Stoics inherited that idea and built on it. So the person who wrongs you isn't a monster who chose evil. They're someone who saw it wrong. Fourth, the result. Starting from this, Epictetus says, you'll be gentle with the one who insults you. And he gives you a short phrase to say each time, only two words in his Greek, a little like a breath before reacting: it seemed so to him. That isn't an excuse for harm. You can still protect yourself, set a limit, even seek justice. What changes is the heat. You stop adding your own anger to their mistake. You see a person who judged badly, not an enemy. And that turns out to be lighter to carry.
screen: `HE DID WHAT SEEMED RIGHT TO HIM.` · `THE ONE DECEIVED IS THE ONE HARMED.` · `NO ONE DOES WRONG KNOWINGLY.` · `SAY IT EACH TIME: IT SEEMED SO TO HIM.` · then, large: `IT SEEMED RIGHT TO HIM.`

segments.voice: Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind someone who wronged you, not the worst, just someone. A sharp email. A broken promise. A rude driver. Now try, for a minute, to stand where they stood. What did it look like from inside their day? What did they believe was true, or fair, or necessary? You don't have to agree. Just look. Then say it quietly: it seemed right to him, or to her, or to them. Notice what happens to the heat. The bell holds the time.
It seemed right to him. Epictetus' short phrase for anyone who wrongs you: they acted on what seemed right to them, and their mistake is their harm. Today's word.
screen: `IT SEEMED RIGHT TO HIM — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: it seemed right to him. Try to understand one wrongdoer today, from the inside of their day, before you decide what to do. Day three hundred seventy-seven.

378.title: The other handle
378.hook: everything has two handles; take your brother by "he is my brother," not "he wronged me" (Enchiridion 43)
378.howItsDone: People practicing Stoicism often reframe a conflict with someone close by starting from the relationship rather than the offense, following Epictetus' image of the two handles.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the driver, the coworker, and the story from inside their day. Your line was it seemed right to him. Whose day did you try to see from the inside? Day three hundred seventy-eight.

A pot on the stove has two handles. One has been sitting over the flame and it's scorching. The other is cool. If you grab the hot one, you drop the pot, and now there's soup on the floor and a burn on your hand. Nobody would blame the pot. You just picked it up by the wrong side. Section forty-three of the handbook is about that choice, and Epictetus aims it straight at family. Today, to end the week: the other handle.
screen: `A POT WITH TWO HANDLES.` → `ONE HOT, ONE COOL.` → `THE OTHER HANDLE.`

segments.voice: First, the line. Everything has two handles, Epictetus says: one by which it can be carried, and one by which it can't. The pot is today's picture, not his, but the handles are his. Second, the brother. If your brother wrongs you, he says, don't take hold of it by the handle he wronged me. That's the handle by which it can't be carried. Take it by the other one: he's my brother, we were raised together. Then you'll be holding it by the handle that can be carried. Third, what changes and what doesn't. The wrong still happened. Epictetus doesn't pretend otherwise. What changes is which fact you pick up first. Grab he wronged me, and every other fact arranges itself around the injury. Grab he's my brother, and the injury becomes one fact inside a longer story, a story with a shared childhood and a kitchen table and probably a few wrongs going the other way. Same situation, different handle, different weight. Fourth, it works beyond brothers. A coworker, a neighbor, a parent, a friend who let you down. Each relationship has its own cool handle: she's been loyal for ten years. He's my father. We've built this together. And a look back at the week, since today closes it: my own size. Mind the step. The foot measures. Honor the character. Mind first. It seemed right to him. Yesterday and today belong together: first you see why they did it, then you choose how to hold it.

segments.voice: Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind one conflict you're carrying, with someone close. Notice which handle you've been holding it by: what they did, what they said, how it hurt. Feel how hot it is. Now, gently, look for the other handle. Who are they to you? What have you shared? What's true about them besides this? Find one fact, and pick the whole thing up by that. Notice the difference in weight. The bell holds the time.
The other handle. Enchiridion forty-three: everything has two handles. Take your brother by he's my brother, not he wronged me. Today's word.
Your line: the other handle. Pick up one conflict today by the other handle: start from who they are to you, not from what they did. Day three hundred seventy-eight.

myth: Epictetus says to pretend the wrong never happened
the wrong is real; you choose which handle to lift it by.
the image of two handles comes from Enchiridion 43
one by which a thing can be carried, one by which it can't.
the hot pot on the stove is Epictetus' own example
the pot is today's picture; his example is the brother who wrongs you.

fork.setup: your brother has wronged you, again. you can feel the hot handle in your hand. what does Epictetus suggest?
options: hold it by he wronged me, so you don't forget.
take it by the other handle: he's my brother, we grew up together.
put it down and never speak to him.
fork.reveal: take it by the handle that can be carried: he's your brother, raised with you. the wrong is still there, but it weighs differently.

original.note: Greek: a handle, a grip. Enchiridion 43 says everything has two.

trapdoor: what you thought: look on the bright side.
what it means: the wrong is real, but you choose which fact to lift it by, and the relationship is the handle that can be carried.
what a scholar hears: labē, a grip or handle; Epictetus' example is a brother 'raised with you', turning a quarrel back into a family.
